## Overview of the Enriched Pathways

In Table 1, the enriched biological pathways are ranked on the basis of statistical significance, biological coherence, and relevance to Alzheimer disease. Several of the strongest signals converge on synaptic and neuronal communication processes, including transmission across chemical synapses (REAC:R-HSA-112315, p = 0.002103704440645029), chemical synaptic transmission (GO:0007268, p = 0.014393306270160168), synaptic vesicle pathway (WP:WP2267, p = 0.012009274435675501), vesicle organization (GO:0016050, p = 0.017522469177414065), and neuronal system (REAC:R-HSA-112316, p = 0.005419267208860265). Taken together, these pathways may indicate a coordinated signal centered on neuronal communication and vesicle-dependent signaling, which is in line with the broader literature suggesting that early synaptic dysfunction, impaired vesicle trafficking, and defective neurotransmitter release are important features of Alzheimer disease and are closely associated with memory loss and cognitive decline.

Extending this pattern, the enrichment of axon-related and neuronal differentiation pathways, including axon (GO:0030424, p = 0.015047975701690239) and cell lineage map for neuronal differentiation (WP:WP5417, p = 0.003930549795925289), may further suggest disruption of neuronal connectivity and maintenance. This interpretation is consistent with evidence indicating that axonal degeneration and altered neuronal identity may contribute to disease progression. In parallel, enrichment of intermediate filament (GO:0005882, p = 0.015047975701690239) points to possible cytoskeletal abnormalities, a biologically relevant observation because filament disorganization and broader cytoskeletal defects have been repeatedly implicated in neurodegeneration and neuronal structural instability in Alzheimer disease.

A related aspect of the enrichment profile involves signaling at the cell surface and in the extracellular environment. The presence of receptor ligand activity (GO:0048018, p = 0.008580190793838793) may suggest altered intercellular signaling, while the highly significant lipoprotein particle receptor binding pathway (GO:0070325, p = 0.0022547284074943743) is particularly notable in view of prior literature linking lipoprotein receptor pathways, especially those involving apolipoprotein signaling and lipid handling, to amyloid biology, neuronal survival, and Alzheimer disease risk. Overall, the pathway profile highlights a coherent disease theme centered on synaptic failure, vesicle and axonal dysfunction, cytoskeletal disruption, and altered receptor-mediated signaling, with low p-values and repeated enrichment across Gene Ontology, WikiPathways, and Reactome providing convergent support for their potential relevance to Alzheimer disease.

## Enriched Pathways Analysis

With this overall pattern in mind, the following sections provide a more detailed discussion of the top enriched pathways.


### vesicle organization (GO:0016050) 

Vesicle organization is the integrated cellular process that governs the biogenesis, assembly, cargo loading, positioning, trafficking, maturation, docking, release, recycling, and degradation of membrane-bounded vesicles. This pathway includes intracellular vesicles that support synaptic transmission, endolysosomal and autophagic vesicles that mediate protein turnover and organelle quality control, dense core secretory vesicles that regulate neuropeptide processing and release, and extracellular vesicles that enable intercellular communication. In the nervous system, proper vesicle organization is essential for maintaining synaptic structure and function because neurotransmission depends on the orderly clustering of synaptic vesicles at presynaptic terminals, their fusion with the plasma membrane, and their subsequent recycling. Vesicle organization is also tightly linked to cellular energetics and acidification, since mitochondrial adenosine triphosphate production and vacuolar proton transport are required for vesicle loading, trafficking, and lysosomal function. In addition, extracellular vesicle production and release shape communication among neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendroglia, and barrier epithelia, thereby influencing inflammatory signaling and the spread of disease-associated proteins. Because this pathway intersects with synaptic homeostasis, proteostasis, lipid metabolism, lysosomal degradation, and cell-to-cell signaling, disruption of vesicle organization has broad consequences for neuronal survival and network integrity.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that vesicle organization may be linked to Alzheimer disease through multiple, partially overlapping levels of pathology, including synaptic failure, amyloid and tau pathology, neuroinflammation, and biomarker release. At the synaptic level, several studies show that Alzheimer disease is associated with disturbed presynaptic vesicle architecture, including reduced synaptic vesicle density, depletion of reserve pools, abnormal enlargement of vesicles, and coupling of these changes to damaged presynaptic mitochondria, supporting the view that defective vesicle organization may represent a structural correlate of synaptic loss and cognitive decline (PubMed:37004141). Consistent with this interpretation, aggregated beta amyloid was shown to cause an initial contraction of the synaptic vesicle cluster followed by synapse loss, whereas tau pathology in experimental systems produced loosened vesicle clustering phenotypes, indicating that both major Alzheimer disease proteinopathies can directly perturb vesicle arrangement at synapses (PubMed:41026542, PubMed:38994745). Molecular studies further connect vesicle dysregulation to disease mechanisms through altered expression of vesicle-related factors, including reduced adenosine triphosphatase hydrogen ion transporting V1 subunit A linked to synaptic vesicle cycle and phagosome pathways, and altered cerebrospinal fluid concentrations of vesicle-associated membrane protein 2 across the Alzheimer disease continuum, findings that are consistent with early and dynamic synaptic vesicle injury (PubMed:33981384, PubMed:37898760).  

Extending from intracellular vesicle defects to extracellular communication, extracellular vesicle biology also appears to be an important component of Alzheimer disease pathogenesis. Structural analysis of postmortem brain tissue identified extracellular vesicles as non-amyloid constituents within beta amyloid plaques, suggesting that vesicle accumulation is physically integrated into plaque microenvironments (PubMed:38987603). Proteomic studies likewise identified vesicle organization as a conserved module within the plaque-associated protein network, together with autophagy and lipid transport, indicating that vesicle remodeling may be a fundamental feature of the amyloid microenvironment (PubMed:41676572). Multiple clinical and experimental studies further show that extracellular vesicle secretion, cargo composition, and physicochemical properties are altered in Alzheimer disease, including changes in vesicle size and concentration, disease-associated protein and micro ribonucleic acid cargoes, and enrichment of inflammatory or astrocyte-derived vesicle signatures that correlate with beta amyloid burden, tau burden, cognitive impairment, and disease stage (PubMed:34046409, PubMed:37834197, PubMed:35029059, PubMed:38071653). Mechanistically, extracellular vesicles appear capable of propagating pathology and inflammation: choroid plexus-derived vesicles are increased by beta amyloid oligomers, carry pro-inflammatory proteins such as complement components, and their inhibition protects against acute beta amyloid oligomer-induced cognitive decline in mice, while reviews synthesize evidence that vesicle-neuron interactions may contribute to early synaptic dysfunction and disease spread (PubMed:34425919, PubMed:36611856, PubMed:40181198). Additional support comes from studies of dense core vesicle cargos, which are aberrantly accumulated in dystrophic neurites and activated astrocytes in Alzheimer disease tissue while declining in cerebrospinal fluid, reinforcing the idea that secretory vesicle organization is disrupted in diseased neural circuits (PubMed:34565482). Taken together, these findings support a cautious model in which impaired vesicle organization may represent more than a secondary bystander phenomenon in Alzheimer disease, potentially linking amyloid and tau toxicity to synaptic disassembly, defective proteostatic and lysosomal handling, altered intercellular communication, inflammatory amplification, and the generation of accessible fluid biomarkers.[PubMed:37004141](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37004141) [PubMed:41026542](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41026542) [PubMed:38994745](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38994745) [PubMed:33981384](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33981384) [PubMed:37898760](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37898760) [PubMed:38987603](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38987603) [PubMed:41676572](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41676572) [PubMed:34046409](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34046409) [PubMed:37834197](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37834197) [PubMed:35029059](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35029059) [PubMed:38071653](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38071653) [PubMed:34425919](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34425919) [PubMed:36611856](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36611856) [PubMed:40181198](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40181198) [PubMed:34565482](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34565482) 

Building on this literature context, the enrichment analysis identified 3 Alzheimer-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of vesicle organization. This enrichment highlights a compact but potentially important functional module, because vesicle organization spans multiple quantitatively critical cellular steps, including vesicle biogenesis, cargo loading, trafficking, docking, release, recycling, and degradation, all of which are essential for neuronal maintenance and are highly relevant to Alzheimer pathobiology through effects on synaptic transmission, lysosomal turnover, extracellular communication, and neuronal survival. The figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 3 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network inspection and evidence review.

To further contextualize these enriched proteins, the following section introduces the significant proteins identified in the functional enrichment analysis in greater detail. APOE is the most notable protein in this list with respect to Alzheimer’s disease because it is the strongest established genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, particularly in the APOE4 isoform. Although the function provided here concerns microbial infection rather than classical lipid transport or amyloid biology, it remains relevant to Alzheimer’s disease mechanisms. Specifically, this entry shows that APOE can mediate pathogen interactions through binding to viral components and through engagement with receptors such as LDLr, VLDLr, and SR-B1, all of which are linked to lipid handling and cellular uptake pathways. This is important because Alzheimer’s disease is increasingly understood to involve not only amyloid-beta and tau pathology, but also dysregulation of lipid metabolism, endocytic trafficking, neuroinflammation, and autophagy. The reported involvement of APOE in HCV attachment and viral particle maturation suggests that APOE can act at the interface between host lipid biology and infectious processes, supporting the broader concept that APOE may influence brain vulnerability through immune and barrier-related mechanisms. In addition, the note that this interaction may be promoted by autophagy is especially interesting, because autophagic dysfunction is a recognized contributor to Alzheimer’s disease pathogenesis. Thus, even though the cited function is derived from a viral infection context, it reinforces the view of APOE as a multifunctional regulator of receptor-mediated uptake, lipid-associated particle biology, and host-response pathways that are mechanistically relevant to Alzheimer’s disease.[PubMed:25122793](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25122793) [PubMed:29695434](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29695434)

### intermediate filament (GO:0005882) 

Intermediate filaments are one of the three principal cytoskeletal systems of eukaryotic cells and form elongated fibers of approximately ten nanometers in diameter that provide tensile strength, structural resilience, and spatial organization to the cytoplasm and nucleus. Unlike actin filaments and microtubules, intermediate filaments are composed of chemically diverse proteins whose expression is highly cell type specific. The major classes include keratins, vimentin-like proteins, neurofilaments, and lamins; in the nervous system, particularly relevant members include neurofilament proteins in neurons and glial fibrillary acidic protein and vimentin in astrocytes. These polymers mechanically integrate cellular compartments, stabilize cell shape, support axonal caliber and conduction, and participate in responses to stress and injury. In the brain, neuronal intermediate filaments are especially important for axonal integrity, whereas astrocytic intermediate filaments are central to reactive gliosis, a state in which astrocytes undergo hypertrophy, transcriptional remodeling, and altered interactions with synapses, blood vessels, and protein aggregates. Taken together, this pathway can be viewed not simply as a static scaffold, but rather as a dynamic system that may reflect and shape neuronal injury, glial activation, tissue remodeling, and proteostatic imbalance, which are all central biological features of Alzheimer disease.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that the intermediate filament pathway is related to Alzheimer disease through two major and biologically connected dimensions: neuronal intermediate filament release as a marker of axonal degeneration, and glial intermediate filament remodeling as an active component of disease pathogenesis. On the neuronal side, neurofilament light chain, a core axonal intermediate filament protein, is consistently elevated in blood and cerebrospinal fluid across the Alzheimer disease continuum, with higher levels in mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer disease than in cognitively healthy individuals, and with stronger elevations accompanying worse cognition and more advanced neurodegeneration. Multiple studies further indicate that increased neurofilament light chain reflects brain atrophy, hypometabolism, white matter injury, disrupted functional connectivity, and future cognitive decline, supporting the interpretation that breakdown of the neuronal intermediate filament network accompanies ongoing axonal injury rather than serving as a disease-specific upstream trigger (PubMed:36625756, PubMed:37540027, PubMed:36574591, PubMed:37519166, PubMed:35102694, PubMed:35806226).  

A complementary line of evidence points to glial intermediate filament remodeling, particularly in astrocytes, as an additional dimension of relevance in Alzheimer disease. On the glial side, glial fibrillary acidic protein, the canonical astrocytic intermediate filament, rises very early in the pathogenic cascade and appears to mediate amyloid-related processes before overt neurodegeneration, while other astrocyte-associated markers help link amyloid deposition to tau phosphorylation and neuronal injury (PubMed:37690071, PubMed:35234335, PubMed:39554381). Beyond its biomarker value, glial fibrillary acidic protein is repeatedly implicated in mechanism: reactive astrocytes in Alzheimer disease show increased intermediate filament expression, and experimental studies suggest that reducing astrogliosis can improve cognition in amyloid mouse models, indicating that astrocytic intermediate filament remodeling may contribute directly to synaptic and network dysfunction (PubMed:33634529). Additional evidence is consistent with this possible pathogenic role, as glial fibrillary acidic protein is overexpressed and differentially phosphorylated in Alzheimer hippocampus, particularly in apolipoprotein E epsilon four homozygotes, and modulation of glial fibrillary acidic protein-associated kinase pathways or direct targeting of glial fibrillary acidic protein reduces aggregate burden in experimental systems (PubMed:35890250). Other intermediate filament family members may also participate: vimentin is increased around amyloid plaques, and its cleavage disrupts the vimentin and glial fibrillary acidic protein network, weakens astrocytic phagocytosis, lowers apolipoprotein E release, and thereby promotes amyloid beta deposition, providing a plausible mechanism by which astrocytic intermediate filament disorganization can impair plaque clearance (PubMed:40243407). In parallel, disease-associated microglial responses in amyloid mouse models involve increased nestin at plaque contact sites, suggesting that intermediate filament remodeling is not restricted to astrocytes but may also support migratory and plaque-interacting states in myeloid cells (PubMed:38802940). Taken together, these studies support a model in which the intermediate filament pathway is closely intertwined with Alzheimer disease: neuronal intermediate filament proteins appear to report the extent of axonal damage and clinical progression, whereas glial intermediate filament proteins may participate in reactive gliosis, amyloid handling, inflammatory remodeling, and downstream neuronal injury, making this pathway relevant both as a source of accessible biomarkers and as a potential therapeutic target.[PubMed:36625756](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36625756) [PubMed:37540027](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37540027) [PubMed:37690071](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37690071) [PubMed:36574591](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36574591) [PubMed:35234335](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35234335) [PubMed:33634529](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33634529) [PubMed:35890250](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35890250) [PubMed:39554381](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39554381) [PubMed:35806226](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35806226) [PubMed:37519166](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37519166) [PubMed:40243407](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40243407) [PubMed:38802940](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38802940) 

Building on this literature context, the enrichment result provides a concise pathway-level summary of these linked neuronal and glial processes. There were 3 Alzheimer disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing intermediate filaments as one of the 3 principal cytoskeletal systems of eukaryotic cells, forming elongated fibers of approximately 10 nanometers in diameter that provide tensile strength, structural resilience, and spatial organization to the cytoplasm and nucleus. This enrichment is biologically notable because the pathway directly links cytoskeletal organization with neuronal integrity, astrocyte reactivity, tissue remodeling, and proteostatic imbalance, all of which are central features of Alzheimer disease. In the brain, the relevance of this pathway is further strengthened by the functional importance of neuronal intermediate filament proteins for axonal caliber and conduction, together with the roles of glial fibrillary acidic protein and vimentin in astrocyte hypertrophy, injury responses, and altered interactions with synapses, blood vessels, and protein aggregates. The figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 3 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided for direct network inspection.

### Cell lineage map for neuronal differentiation (WP:WP5417) 

The cell lineage map for neuronal differentiation describes the ordered progression by which stem cells and progenitor cells commit to a neuronal fate, proliferate, exit the cell cycle, differentiate into immature neurons, extend neurites, acquire synaptic competence, and finally mature into functionally integrated neuronal subtypes. This pathway is not a single linear molecular cascade, but rather a developmental framework that integrates cell state transitions with regulatory signals from intrinsic transcription factors, extracellular niche cues, and intercellular communication. In the adult and developing nervous system, neuronal lineage progression typically begins with neural stem cells or related progenitors, proceeds through transit-amplifying precursor states and neuroblasts, and culminates in postmitotic neurons with region-specific identities. The publications provided suggest that this lineage progression is tightly regulated by signaling systems such as wingless-related integration site signaling, cell cycle regulators, and local niche-derived factors. For example, single-cell profiling of the adult ventricular-subventricular zone identified a progenitor intermediate enriched for notum pectinacetylesterase homolog, a secreted antagonist of wingless-related integration site signaling, demonstrating that context-dependent modulation of proliferation is a core feature of neuronal lineage control (PubMed:32579931). Additional studies indicate that genes such as forkhead box G1 coordinate stem cell activation, precursor expansion, and neuronal differentiation, whereas beta-secretase 1 and cyclin-dependent kinase 5 influence the balance between proliferation, differentiation, and neurite development during neuronal maturation (PubMed:40297942, PubMed:30079376, PubMed:38937422). Taken together, the pathway may be best understood as a dynamic lineage architecture in which developmental competence, environmental signals, and disease-associated stressors jointly influence whether neural precursor populations successfully generate mature neurons.  

Against this developmental background, the relevance of the pathway to Alzheimer disease becomes more apparent because the disease appears to affect not only mature neurons but also the cellular programs that generate, maintain, and mature neuronal lineages, thereby linking neurodegeneration with impaired endogenous repair. A key line of evidence comes from induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neuronal differentiation models, in which Down syndrome-derived neurons rapidly developed amyloid deposition, tau hyperphosphorylation, and tau mislocalization during lineage progression, showing that Alzheimer-like pathology can emerge early as neurons differentiate and mature; notably, treatment that enhanced canonical wingless-related integration site signaling reduced amyloid beta and tau pathology, directly connecting neuronal differentiation control with Alzheimer-relevant mechanisms (PubMed:25735452). In aging primate entorhinal cortex, single-nucleus transcriptomics further showed that the neuronal lineage is among the cell populations most affected by aging and is especially prone to Alzheimer disease, with increased amyloid precursor protein and microtubule-associated protein tau expression across aged cell types and a particularly vulnerable excitatory neuronal subpopulation, indicating that age-related remodeling of neuronal lineage states may create a permissive context for Alzheimer pathology (PubMed:36165462). Experimental studies also suggest that regulators of lineage progression are mechanistically tied to Alzheimer disease biology: forkhead box G1 overexpression in an Alzheimer model promoted neural stem cell activation, precursor proliferation, neuroblast differentiation, and hippocampal neuron generation while improving cognition and reducing pathological deficits, supporting the possibility that restoring neuronal lineage progression may counter disease manifestations (PubMed:40297942). Conversely, beta-secretase 1 deficiency increased precursor proliferation but impaired differentiation into the neuronal lineage, leaving a pool of undifferentiated progenitors, which is important because beta-secretase 1 is a major therapeutic target in Alzheimer disease and these findings imply that excessive suppression of this enzyme could adversely affect adult hippocampal neurogenesis (PubMed:30079376). Additional evidence indicates that amyloid beta itself exerts complex lineage effects: in subventricular zone neurospheres, amyloid beta forty-two promoted differentiation of progenitors toward neuronal fates through deoxyribonucleic acid polymerase beta, suggesting that Alzheimer-associated proteins can aberrantly reshape lineage decisions even while damaging mature neurons (PubMed:22057776). Broader contextual studies further reinforce this interpretation, including the proposal that tanycyte-derived neurogenesis may be impaired in Alzheimer disease and thereby exacerbate neurodegeneration, as well as evidence that astrocyte-neuron interactions reprogram neuronal gene regulatory networks enriched for genes implicated in autosomal dominant Alzheimer disease, underscoring the importance of the lineage microenvironment for neuronal maturation and vulnerability (PubMed:38934388, PubMed:41867870). Collectively, these studies suggest that the cell lineage map for neuronal differentiation is highly relevant to Alzheimer disease because the disorder may disrupt multiple stages of neuronal lineage progression, from stem cell activation and progenitor proliferation to terminal differentiation and neuronal maturation, while disease-associated molecules such as amyloid beta, tau-related processes, and niche signaling pathways feed back onto this lineage system to influence both vulnerability and regenerative capacity.[PubMed:25735452](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25735452) [PubMed:32579931](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32579931) [PubMed:36165462](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36165462) [PubMed:40297942](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40297942) [PubMed:30079376](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30079376) [PubMed:22057776](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22057776) [PubMed:38934388](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38934388) [PubMed:38937422](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38937422) [PubMed:41867870](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41867870) 

Building on this biological context, the enrichment result can be interpreted within the broader developmental structure of the pathway. There were 3 Alzheimer disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway describing the cell lineage map for neuronal differentiation. This enrichment is notable because the pathway captures a multistage developmental continuum, beginning with stem cell commitment and progenitor expansion and ending with postmitotic neuronal maturation, neurite extension, synaptic competence acquisition, and functional integration. In the context of Alzheimer disease, the identification of 3 proteins within this lineage framework supports the view that disease biology is linked not only to neuronal degeneration at late stages, but also to dysregulation across earlier cellular transitions that govern neuronal production, differentiation timing, and maturation capacity. The pathway description further indicates that this developmental architecture is quantitatively shaped by regulatory systems controlling proliferation and differentiation, including wingless-related integration site signaling antagonism through notum pectinacetylesterase homolog in progenitor intermediates, as well as the actions of forkhead box G1, beta-secretase 1, and cyclin-dependent kinase 5 on stem cell activation, precursor expansion, neuronal differentiation, and neurite development (PubMed:32579931). Additional evidence from the cited studies supports a model in which lineage progression is not linear but dynamically regulated by intrinsic transcriptional programs, extracellular niche signals, and disease-associated stress, thereby increasing the biological relevance of even a relatively small enriched protein set of 3 when mapped onto a pathway spanning multiple sequential cell states from progenitors to mature neurons (PubMed:40297942, PubMed:30079376, PubMed:38937422). Accordingly, we include the protein-protein interaction network visualization below together with the corresponding Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes and Proteins webpage link for direct inspection of the 3 enriched proteins and their interaction structure.

### chemical synaptic transmission (GO:0007268) 

Chemical synaptic transmission is the fundamental biological process through which neurons communicate at chemical synapses. The process begins when an action potential reaches the presynaptic terminal and induces membrane depolarization, which opens voltage-sensitive calcium channels. The resulting calcium influx promotes docking, priming, and fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic membrane through the vesicle exocytosis machinery, thereby releasing neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft. These neurotransmitters then bind ionotropic or metabotropic receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, altering membrane potential, intracellular ionic composition, and downstream signaling pathways. This pathway also includes spontaneous neurotransmitter release, neurotransmitter reuptake and recycling, presynaptic transporter activity, receptor localization and stabilization at the postsynaptic specialization, and the molecular systems that maintain excitation and inhibition balance. Because learning, memory encoding, network synchronization, and activity-dependent plasticity all depend on efficient synaptic signaling, chemical synaptic transmission is closely linked to dendritic spine integrity, synaptic vesicle cycling, calcium homeostasis, receptor trafficking, inhibitory interneuron function, and cholinergic, glutamatergic, and gamma-aminobutyric acid mediated neurotransmission. Accordingly, disruption of any of these components can impair synaptic efficacy and circuit function, which makes this pathway especially relevant to neurodegenerative disorders in which synaptic failure is an early and major pathological event.  

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that chemical synaptic transmission is not merely a secondary consequence of Alzheimer disease, but may represent a central pathway through which molecular pathology is translated into circuit dysfunction, cognitive decline, and disease progression. Systems-level studies show that genes linked to chemical synaptic transmission are consistently enriched in Alzheimer disease-related structural and connectomic abnormalities, including disease-specific brain gradient changes, altered morphological connectivity, and cortical thinning during progression from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer disease. These observations suggest that synaptic signaling programs are tightly coupled to the anatomical vulnerability of affected brain regions (PubMed:39392880, PubMed:37846762, PubMed:34776930). Mechanistically, several studies connect this pathway to core Alzheimer disease lesions. Tau pathology has been described as a direct driver of synaptic proteome disruption and functional abnormalities of synaptic transmission, supporting the view that Alzheimer disease may be fundamentally a synaptic disorder in which synapse loss and synaptic dysfunction closely track cognitive impairment (PubMed:28123806). In parallel, integrated epigenomic and transcriptomic analysis identified dysregulated genes enriched in chemical synaptic transmission and proposed transforming growth factor beta receptor three as a risk factor that may promote amyloid beta production while acting through synaptic vesicle cycling, calcium signaling, and related synaptic regulators, thereby linking amyloidogenic processing to presynaptic and postsynaptic dysfunction (PubMed:35310542). Additional transcriptomic network work implicated long non-coding ribonucleic acid regulation in pathways such as calcium-regulated neurotransmitter exocytosis, presynaptic membrane assembly, receptor localization to synapses, and learning, again placing synaptic transmission near the center of Alzheimer disease biology (PubMed:31755891). Functional evidence from animal and cellular models further strengthens this relationship. In early-stage amyloid precursor protein and presenilin one mutant mice, impaired gamma-aminobutyric acid transmission in the hippocampus, loss of parvalbumin interneurons, and reduced neurotransmitter synthesis and transport produced hyperexcitability, excitation-inhibition imbalance, and increased seizure susceptibility, while neuregulin one treatment improved both seizures and cognition, demonstrating that restoration of inhibitory synaptic transmission can rescue Alzheimer disease-related phenotypes (PubMed:38388921). Human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived hippocampal spheroids carrying Alzheimer disease-associated variants also showed reduced synaptic protein levels and altered expression of genes involved in synaptic transmission, consistent with early intrinsic synaptic defects in vulnerable hippocampal tissue (PubMed:32589876). At the level of molecular profiling, single-synapse transcriptomics revealed Alzheimer disease-associated synaptic gene expression changes that were not detectable by nucleus-based approaches, emphasizing that pathogenic alterations are concentrated within synaptic compartments themselves (PubMed:36646931). Clinical biomarker studies are concordant with these observations, showing reduced synaptophysin in circulating small extracellular vesicles from mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer disease together with increased amyloid beta, phosphorylated tau, and inflammatory markers, indicating that synaptic degeneration and neuroinflammation evolve together during disease progression (PubMed:38902659). Therapeutic studies also repeatedly converge on this pathway: copper chelation restored proteins related to the cholinergic system and synaptic transmission in a transgenic mouse model, while other pharmacological and multi-component interventions improved cognition in association with restoration of synaptic transmission and neurotransmitter function (PubMed:36221993, PubMed:40202070). Collectively, these findings support a model in which amyloid beta, tau, epigenetic dysregulation, non-coding ribonucleic acid networks, calcium imbalance, inhibitory interneuron loss, and inflammatory signaling converge on chemical synaptic transmission, producing early synaptic failure that may contribute to memory impairment, network instability, and progressive neurodegeneration in Alzheimer disease.[PubMed:39392880](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39392880) [PubMed:38388921](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38388921) [PubMed:35310542](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35310542) [PubMed:31755891](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31755891) [PubMed:34776930](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34776930) [PubMed:28123806](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28123806) [PubMed:40043785](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40043785) [PubMed:37846762](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37846762) [PubMed:32589876](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32589876) [PubMed:36646931](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36646931) [PubMed:38902659](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38902659) [PubMed:36221993](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36221993) [PubMed:40202070](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40202070) 

Building on this literature context, the enrichment analysis provides a more focused view of the proteins associated with this pathway in the present dataset. There were 4 Alzheimer disease-associated proteins identified in the function enrichment analysis for the pathway “chemical synaptic transmission,” a core neuronal communication process that is highly relevant to Alzheimer disease because synaptic dysfunction is an early and major pathological feature of the disorder. Given that the enriched set contains 4 proteins, this observation supports a focused but biologically meaningful convergence on mechanisms governing neurotransmitter release, calcium-dependent vesicle fusion, postsynaptic receptor signaling, neurotransmitter recycling, and excitation-inhibition balance, all of which are quantitatively central to learning, memory formation, and circuit stability in the diseased brain. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 4 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network inspection and evidence review.

To further clarify the biological relevance of the enriched set, the significant proteins identified in the analysis are discussed below in greater detail. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the proteins listed, apolipoprotein E is by far the most directly and compellingly connected to Alzheimer disease. Although the function provided here concerns microbial infection and hepatitis C virus biology, it remains highly relevant to Alzheimer disease because apolipoprotein E is a central regulator of lipid transport, receptor interactions, and neurobiological homeostasis in the brain. Apolipoprotein E is the strongest common genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer disease, particularly the apolipoprotein E epsilon 4 allele, which has been extensively linked to amyloid beta aggregation, impaired amyloid clearance, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier abnormalities. The infection-related function described here is notable because it highlights apolipoprotein E ability to mediate ligand-receptor interactions through low-density lipoprotein receptor family members and scavenger receptor class B member 1, pathways that overlap conceptually with mechanisms relevant to neuronal lipid trafficking and amyloid handling. In addition, the mention of autophagy is especially important, as defective autophagy is a recognized contributor to Alzheimer disease pathogenesis through impaired clearance of toxic protein aggregates, including amyloid beta and tau. Thus, even though the cited function is framed in the context of hepatitis C virus infection, it reinforces broader biological properties of apolipoprotein E, namely receptor-dependent particle handling, lipid-associated trafficking, and links to autophagic processes, all of which are highly pertinent to Alzheimer disease mechanisms.[PubMed:25122793](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25122793) [PubMed:29695434](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29695434) 

In comparison with apolipoprotein E, VGF appears to have a less direct and less established connection to Alzheimer disease in the context of the function provided here. VGF stands out less directly than apolipoprotein E in relation to Alzheimer disease, and the function provided here appears atypical for canonical VGF biology, as it describes a complement component 3a-responsive inflammatory receptor activity more commonly associated with complement-mediated immune signaling. Interpreted cautiously and at face value, however, this function may still be relevant to Alzheimer disease because complement activation, chemotaxis, oxidative burst, and inflammatory cell recruitment are important features of Alzheimer-associated neuroinflammation. The stimulation of chemotaxis, granule enzyme release, and superoxide anion production points to innate immune activation and oxidative stress, both of which are strongly implicated in neuronal injury and synaptic loss in Alzheimer disease. If this annotation reflects a complement-linked inflammatory pathway, its relevance would lie in the growing recognition that dysregulated complement signaling contributes to microglial activation and neurodegenerative progression. Nevertheless, based on the information provided, the Alzheimer disease connection for VGF is more indirect and less established than for apolipoprotein E. Therefore, VGF may be considered of secondary interest here, primarily through its possible association with inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms that can exacerbate Alzheimer pathology.

### receptor ligand activity (GO:0048018) 

Receptor ligand activity refers to the molecular function by which a gene product binds to a receptor and alters receptor state, signaling output, or downstream cellular behavior. This is a foundational mechanism of intercellular communication in multicellular tissues, including the brain, where secreted proteins, membrane-tethered ligands, immune mediators, neurotransmitter-related molecules, and checkpoint ligands regulate neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, glial activation, vascular integrity, and immune trafficking. In the central nervous system, receptor ligand activity is especially important because communication between neurons, microglia, astrocytes, oligodendroglial lineage cells, endothelial cells, and infiltrating immune cells depends on precisely coordinated ligand-receptor interactions. These interactions can trigger forward signaling in receptor-expressing cells as well as reverse signaling in ligand-bearing cells, thereby shaping both cell-autonomous and multicellular responses. In Alzheimer disease, this pathway is highly relevant because disease progression involves disturbed communication across the neurovascular unit, altered glia-neuron signaling, maladaptive immune checkpoint signaling, and changes in microglial inhibitory receptor engagement. Thus, receptor ligand activity provides a unifying framework for understanding how extracellular cues are converted into intracellular programs that influence amyloid pathology, tau phosphorylation, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier impairment, and cognitive decline.  

Against this biological background, the collected publications suggest that receptor ligand activity may be related to Alzheimer disease through several convergent mechanisms involving neuroimmune communication, glia-neuron crosstalk, and neurovascular dysfunction. A particularly direct example is provided by the Alzheimer disease-associated variant of ephrin type-A receptor 1, in which the Proline to Leucine substitution reduced receptor membrane and soluble abundance, impaired ligand-induced phosphorylation, and weakened reverse signaling to brain endothelial cells, leading to altered T-cell recruitment and loss of normal blood-brain barrier regulatory effects. These findings connect defective receptor ligand signaling to vascular and inflammatory processes relevant to late-onset Alzheimer disease. At the broader tissue level, single-nucleus ribonucleic acid sequencing analysis of human cortex showed that ligand-receptor communication between glia and neurons is altered in a cell-type-specific manner in Alzheimer disease, with involvement of amyloid beta precursor protein and apolipoprotein E and downstream perturbation of Wingless-related integration site, tumor protein fifty-three, and nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells signaling in inhibitory neurons. This observation supports the view that disrupted receptor ligand activity may contribute to abnormal transcriptional states and neuronal vulnerability. Additional evidence comes from microglial inhibitory receptor biology: loss of paired immunoglobulin-like type 2 receptor alpha improved microglial immunometabolism, chemotaxis, and stress resistance, reduced amyloid pathology, and rescued synaptic markers in experimental models, while antibody-based ligand blockade phenocopied receptor loss. These findings suggest that pathological engagement of an inhibitory receptor-ligand axis may worsen Alzheimer-related phenotypes and that modulation of this interaction could be therapeutically relevant. Immune checkpoint signaling provides another link, as programmed cell death protein 1 and programmed cell death ligand 1 were upregulated in multiple Alzheimer disease models, correlated with glycogen synthase kinase three beta activity, and blockade of programmed cell death protein 1 reduced both glycogen synthase kinase three beta activity and tau hyperphosphorylation while improving memory. This pattern suggests that aberrant receptor ligand activity may directly influence a core tau-related pathogenic mechanism. Although several other listed studies focus primarily on drug discovery rather than disease mechanism, they further underscore the disease relevance of receptor ligand activity by targeting receptor-directed interactions such as nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and sigma receptors in efforts to restore synaptic and cognitive function in Alzheimer disease. Taken together, these studies support the interpretation that Alzheimer disease may be associated not simply with altered abundance of receptors or ligands in isolation, but with a broader disturbance of receptor ligand activity across neuronal, glial, immune, and vascular compartments, with plausible consequences for amyloid accumulation, tau dysregulation, inflammatory imbalance, barrier dysfunction, and synaptic decline.[PubMed:38184788](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38184788) [PubMed:38849813](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38849813) [PubMed:41337541](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41337541) [PubMed:34977020](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34977020) [PubMed:30296684](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30296684) [PubMed:32935187](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32935187) [PubMed:39559892](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39559892) 

Consistent with this literature-based context, there were 3 Alzheimer disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of receptor ligand activity. This functional category is highly relevant to Alzheimer disease because it captures extracellular signaling events that regulate receptor activation, downstream signal transduction, and multicellular communication across neurons, microglia, astrocytes, oligodendroglial lineage cells, endothelial cells, and infiltrating immune cells. Even with a relatively small set of 3 proteins, the enrichment appears biologically informative because receptor ligand activity represents a core molecular mechanism through which altered intercellular signaling can influence amyloid pathology, tau phosphorylation, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier impairment, and cognitive decline in Alzheimer disease. Figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 3 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here for direct network exploration.

![PPI Network](imgs/c0a06c94-0409-4bd4-a7a2-da74494666fd.png)
![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=9DF4222E6EDAD05C)

With this pathway-level overview in place, the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis can be considered individually. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  

Among the listed proteins, apolipoprotein E is the most directly and compellingly linked to Alzheimer disease. Apolipoprotein E is already a central genetic and mechanistic factor in Alzheimer pathogenesis, particularly through its established roles in lipid transport, amyloid-beta aggregation and clearance, neuroinflammation, and blood-brain barrier integrity. The function described here is notable because it highlights apolipoprotein E as a host factor in viral attachment and infectivity, suggesting a broader role in host-pathogen interactions. This is relevant to Alzheimer disease because infectious and innate immune hypotheses of neurodegeneration propose that microbial exposure, antiviral responses, and chronic inflammation may contribute to amyloid deposition and neuronal injury. In addition, the mention of autophagy is important, as defective autophagic flux is a recognized feature of Alzheimer disease and is closely tied to abnormal protein aggregation and neuronal stress. Thus, this function reinforces the concept that apolipoprotein E may influence Alzheimer disease not only through classical lipid and amyloid pathways but also through infection-related and autophagy-associated mechanisms that could modulate neurodegenerative vulnerability.[PubMed:25122793](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25122793) [PubMed:29695434](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29695434) 

In a somewhat different but potentially complementary way, growth differentiation factor 15 also stands out as a relevant protein in Alzheimer disease because it is a stress-responsive signaling factor with strong effects on brainstem circuits, systemic metabolism, and cellular signaling pathways that are frequently altered in neurodegeneration. Although growth differentiation factor 15 is not a canonical Alzheimer gene in the same way as apolipoprotein E, its described functions intersect with several disease-relevant domains. First, its induction by diverse stresses, including cancer, drugs, and metabolic perturbation, suggests that it may act as a marker and mediator of organismal stress responses, which are highly pertinent to aging and neurodegeneration. Second, its signaling through rearranged during transfection, mitogen-activated protein kinase, and protein kinase B pathways connects it to survival, inflammatory, and metabolic programs that may influence neuronal resilience or degeneration. Third, the regulation of appetite and lipid metabolism is relevant because weight loss, metabolic dysfunction, and altered energy homeostasis are common features in Alzheimer disease, often appearing before advanced cognitive decline. Therefore, growth differentiation factor 15 may be mechanistically linked to Alzheimer disease through systemic stress signaling, neuro-metabolic dysfunction, and maladaptive central responses to chronic disease states.[PubMed:28846097](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846097) [PubMed:28846098](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846098) [PubMed:28846099](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28846099) [PubMed:28953886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28953886) [PubMed:31152154](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31152154) [PubMed:31875646](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31875646) [PubMed:31928886](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31928886) [PubMed:32661391](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32661391) [PubMed:32723474](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723474) [PubMed:33593916](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33593916) [PubMed:35202387](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35202387) [PubMed:36630958](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36630958) [PubMed:37380764](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37380764) 

Finally, the third protein entry is potentially relevant to Alzheimer disease because the annotated function centers on complement component 3a-mediated inflammatory signaling, and complement activation is increasingly recognized as a major driver of Alzheimer pathology. The complement component 3a axis is associated with immune-cell recruitment, oxidative burst, and inflammatory effector responses, all of which can contribute to chronic neuroinflammation, synaptic injury, and neuronal dysfunction in the Alzheimer brain. In particular, excessive complement activity has been implicated in maladaptive synapse elimination by microglia and amplification of tissue-damaging inflammatory cascades. Therefore, a protein participating in complement component 3a-responsive chemotactic and oxidative pathways could plausibly influence Alzheimer-related neuroimmune mechanisms. However, compared with apolipoprotein E, the connection is less direct based on the provided annotation alone, and the functional description should be interpreted cautiously in the absence of additional Alzheimer-specific evidence in the supplied text.

### Synaptic vesicle pathway (WP:WP2267) 

The synaptic vesicle pathway comprises the presynaptic processes that govern the formation, loading, trafficking, docking, priming, calcium-triggered fusion, endocytic retrieval, recycling, and degradation of synaptic vesicles. Through this pathway, neurotransmitters are packaged into membrane-bound vesicles, mobilized to active zones, released into the synaptic cleft in response to electrical activity, and then replenished through tightly coordinated membrane trafficking steps. Core components include vesicle membrane proteins, fusion machinery, calcium sensors, endocytic adaptors, proton pumps, and regulators of vesicle identity and recycling. Because this pathway sustains neurotransmission and short-term synaptic plasticity, even subtle disturbances can impair circuit function before overt neuronal death occurs. In the context of Alzheimer disease, the synaptic vesicle pathway is especially important because synaptic failure is one of the earliest and strongest correlates of cognitive decline. The pathway also intersects with amyloid precursor protein processing, endocytic trafficking, mitochondrial energy supply, glial-mediated synapse remodeling, and inflammatory signaling, thereby placing it at the center of mechanisms that may connect protein aggregation, presynaptic dysfunction, and progressive neurodegeneration. 

With this biological context in mind, the studies summarized below collectively suggest that the synaptic vesicle pathway may represent a major site at which Alzheimer disease pathology is initiated, amplified, and potentially therapeutically modified. Human transcriptomic and spatial atlas studies show that Alzheimer disease brains exhibit broad disruption of synaptic and vesicle-related programs together with regional synapse loss, especially in vulnerable hippocampal fields, while inflammatory glial responses and synapse pruning are spatially concentrated around amyloid beta deposits, indicating that presynaptic injury occurs within a neuroimmune microenvironment rather than in isolation (PubMed:40168986). Multiple expression and network analyses further identify synaptic vesicle cycling, vesicle metabolism, and related synaptic signaling pathways among the most consistently altered molecular signatures in affected cortex and hippocampus, with several vesicle-associated genes proposed as biomarkers or protective factors, including adenosine triphosphatase hydrogen ion transporting V one subunit D, adenosine triphosphatase hydrogen ion transporting V one subunit G two, clathrin light chain B, N ethylmaleimide sensitive factor, and ubiquitin conjugating enzyme E two N, many of which are reduced in Alzheimer disease and inversely associated with inflammatory infiltration (PubMed:40021385, PubMed:39987324, PubMed:31256118, PubMed:35096262). Mechanistically, amyloid beta oligomers directly perturb presynaptic function by driving abnormal calcium channel activity and pathological enhancement of evoked synaptic vesicle exocytosis, thereby producing dysfunctional neurotransmitter release rather than normal synaptic signaling (PubMed:40127100). In parallel, presynaptic vesicle biology appears to influence amyloid generation itself: synaptic vesicle protein two A is reduced in Alzheimer disease hippocampus, colocalizes with amyloid precursor protein, and its deficiency promotes increased amyloid beta and tau phosphorylation, whereas its overexpression suppresses genes linked to amyloidogenic processing and lipid risk pathways (PubMed:34277597). Consistent with this interpretation, levetiracetam was shown in animal models to lower amyloid beta forty two by synaptic vesicle protein two A-dependent modulation of synaptic vesicle cycling and amyloid precursor protein trafficking, shifting amyloid precursor protein toward non-amyloidogenic processing while restoring presynaptic abnormalities and reducing synapse loss (PubMed:41671338). These observations also align with earlier and broader trafficking literature showing that amyloid precursor protein processing is closely tied to endocytic membrane traffic and that endocytic dysfunction can secondarily impair synaptic vesicle transport and neurotransmitter release, even though amyloid precursor protein itself is enriched mainly in Rab five-positive vesicular organelles distinct from canonical synaptic vesicles (PubMed:28697973, PubMed:8943215). Additional studies indicate that vesicle release machinery is vulnerable to disease-associated stressors: chronic hypoperfusion elevates micro ribonucleic acid one hundred fifty three, which suppresses synaptosomal associated protein twenty five, vesicle associated membrane protein two, syntaxin one A, and synaptotagmin one, blunting vesicle exocytosis and worsening memory-related physiology, a mechanism that may be relevant to Alzheimer disease and vascular contributions to dementia (PubMed:32252776). From a therapeutic perspective, both mechanistic and clinical studies suggest that this pathway may be modifiable: dauricine improved cognition in a transgenic model while altering synapse-related proteins and enriching the synaptic vesicle cycle alongside mitochondrial metabolism pathways, and cerebrospinal fluid proteomics from a clinical trial of zervimesine identified treatment-responsive proteins linked to synapses and vesicle trafficking that correlated with improved electrophysiological connectivity (PubMed:33634105, PubMed:40547328). Finally, the synaptic vesicle pathway is tightly coupled to glial and peripheral immune mechanisms that shape disease progression, because excessive complement-dependent synaptic pruning by activated microglia, including pruning induced by gut-derived bacterial vesicles carrying lipopolysaccharide, likely removes structurally and functionally compromised synapses already weakened by presynaptic vesicle dysfunction (PubMed:40731189, PubMed:41745721). Taken together, the available evidence supports a cautious model in which Alzheimer disease may involve a reciprocal cycle: amyloid and inflammatory stress disrupt synaptic vesicle trafficking and release, defective vesicle and endocytic pathways further favor amyloidogenic processing and synaptic instability, and glial pruning then accelerates the loss of vulnerable connections that underlies cognitive decline.[PubMed:40168986](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40168986) [PubMed:40547328](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40547328) [PubMed:41671338](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41671338) [PubMed:34277597](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34277597) [PubMed:40731189](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40731189) [PubMed:32252776](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32252776) [PubMed:8943215](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8943215) [PubMed:28697973](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28697973) [PubMed:40127100](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40127100) [PubMed:31256118](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31256118) [PubMed:35096262](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35096262) [PubMed:40021385](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40021385) [PubMed:39987324](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39987324) [PubMed:33634105](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33634105) [PubMed:41745721](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41745721) 

Building on this literature-based interpretation, the enrichment result provides a focused network-level view of how this pathway may be represented in the present dataset. There were 2 Alzheimer disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the synaptic vesicle pathway, a presynaptic system that spans vesicle formation, neurotransmitter loading, trafficking, docking, priming, calcium-triggered membrane fusion, endocytic retrieval, recycling, and degradation. Although the enriched set is numerically small, with a protein count of 2, this pathway remains biologically important in Alzheimer disease because synaptic dysfunction is among the earliest pathological changes and is strongly associated with cognitive decline. Therefore, even a limited protein representation within this pathway may still indicate potentially meaningful disruption of neurotransmission-related processes in disease-relevant molecular networks. The figure below illustrates the protein-protein interaction network of these 2 proteins, and the corresponding STRING webpage is provided here: [Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=16189FA6FC9504E6).

### lipoprotein particle receptor binding (GO:0070325) 

Lipoprotein particle receptor binding is the molecular process by which a ligand, most commonly an apolipoprotein or a lipoprotein-associated complex, physically engages a cell-surface receptor that recognizes lipoprotein particles. In the nervous system, this pathway is central to the trafficking of cholesterol, phospholipids, cholesteryl esters, and other hydrophobic cargoes that cannot move efficiently in aqueous extracellular environments without carrier particles. Major ligands participating in this process include apolipoprotein E and clusterin, which decorate lipoprotein particles and confer receptor specificity, while major receptors include low-density lipoprotein receptor, low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1, very low-density lipoprotein receptor, and triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2. Binding of lipoprotein particles or apolipoprotein-containing complexes to these receptors initiates receptor-mediated uptake, intracellular sorting, lysosomal delivery, receptor recycling, and, in some cases, signal transduction that influences neuronal survival, synaptic maintenance, microglial phagocytosis, and vascular clearance. In the brain, this pathway is especially important because local lipid homeostasis is tightly coupled to membrane turnover, myelin maintenance, synapse remodeling, and proteostasis. The functional consequences of receptor binding depend strongly on apolipoprotein isoform, lipidation state, receptor identity, and cellular context. These variables determine whether receptor engagement promotes beneficial clearance of amyloid beta and lipid debris or instead enhances endolysosomal stress, lipid peroxidation, tau accumulation, and neurodegeneration. Thus, lipoprotein particle receptor binding represents a mechanistic intersection between lipid metabolism, protein aggregation, innate immunity, and clearance biology in Alzheimer disease.

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that lipoprotein particle receptor binding may be closely and multifactorially linked to Alzheimer disease because the same receptor-ligand interactions that normally support brain lipid transport and waste clearance also regulate amyloid beta handling, tau pathology, lysosomal integrity, and microglial responses. A central theme is the interaction between apolipoprotein E-containing lipoproteins and members of the low-density lipoprotein receptor family. Low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 has been repeatedly identified as a major receptor for amyloid beta and apolipoprotein E, and its receptor-mediated uptake appears to contribute importantly to brain amyloid beta clearance in neurons, glia, vascular cells, and even in the periphery through hepatic clearance mechanisms; reduction of hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 increases brain amyloid burden and worsens behavioral phenotypes in mouse models, emphasizing that impaired receptor binding and clearance may promote disease progression (PubMed:24904407; PubMed:38885850; PubMed:15959937). In parallel, apolipoprotein E isoform biology strongly implicates this pathway in disease risk. The apolipoprotein E4 isoform is the strongest common genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer disease, whereas apolipoprotein E2 is protective, and recent work shows that reduced binding of lipidated apolipoprotein E2 to low-density lipoprotein receptor prevents receptor recycling defects, decreases neuronal uptake of cholesteryl esters, and limits lipofuscin formation, lysosomal pathology, and tau fibril accumulation; notably, the protective Christchurch variant similarly reduces receptor binding, directly suggesting that attenuated lipoprotein particle receptor binding can be beneficial in the setting of pathogenic lipid cargoes (PubMed:39532095). Earlier mechanistic work further connects apolipoprotein E to tau by showing that apolipoprotein E3, but not apolipoprotein E4, binds tau through the receptor-binding domain of apolipoprotein E, implying that structural features governing receptor interactions are also relevant to tau metabolism and neurofibrillary pathology (PubMed:7972031). 

A further layer of evidence comes from microglial and ligand-composition studies, which extend this pathway beyond neuronal uptake alone. Triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 2 binds apolipoproteins including apolipoprotein E and clusterin and facilitates uptake of lipoproteins and amyloid beta-lipoprotein complexes, whereas Alzheimer disease-associated variants weaken this binding and reduce uptake, supporting a model in which defective receptor engagement may compromise microglial clearance of amyloid beta (PubMed:27477018). Consistent with this possibility, very low-density lipoprotein receptor is expressed in neurons and plaque-associated microglia and has been proposed to participate in metabolism of apolipoprotein E and apolipoprotein E-amyloid beta complexes in Alzheimer brain (PubMed:8786409). The pathway is also shaped upstream by lipoprotein particle composition: adenosine triphosphate-binding cassette transporter A1 promotes apolipoprotein E lipidation, and enhancement of this axis improves apolipoprotein E function and ameliorates amyloid-related phenotypes, indicating that the quality of the ligand presented for receptor binding influences downstream pathogenic or protective outcomes (PubMed:20188211; PubMed:39191400). Clusterin similarly participates in lipoprotein particles, binds amyloid beta, and promotes receptor-mediated endocytosis by glial cells, further linking lipoprotein receptor binding to amyloid disposal (PubMed:19651157). Taken together, these studies suggest that Alzheimer disease may be strongly influenced by the efficiency and quality of lipoprotein particle receptor binding: when this pathway supports balanced lipid transport and amyloid beta clearance it may be protective, but when altered by apolipoprotein E isoform, receptor dysfunction, abnormal lipid cargo, or impaired microglial recognition, it may promote amyloid accumulation, lysosomal injury, tau pathology, and neurodegeneration.[PubMed:7972031](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7972031) [PubMed:27477018](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27477018) [PubMed:24904407](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24904407) [PubMed:38885850](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38885850) [PubMed:15959937](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15959937) [PubMed:8786409](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8786409) [PubMed:20188211](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20188211) [PubMed:19651157](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19651157) [PubMed:39191400](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39191400) [PubMed:39532095](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39532095) 

This literature-based context helps clarify why the enrichment result, although numerically small, may still be biologically informative. There were 2 Alzheimer disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of lipoprotein particle receptor binding. This enrichment highlights a highly focused functional signal, because the implicated process is defined by direct molecular engagement between lipoprotein-associated ligands and cell-surface receptors that regulate lipid transport, receptor-mediated uptake, intracellular sorting, lysosomal delivery, receptor recycling, and downstream signaling in the nervous system. In the context of Alzheimer disease, this pathway is quantitatively important because it sits at the intersection of 4 major pathological domains described for the disease process, namely lipid metabolism, protein aggregation, innate immunity, and clearance biology. The biological relevance of this enrichment is further strengthened by the fact that altered receptor binding of apolipoprotein-decorated particles can shift cellular outcomes toward either improved clearance of amyloid beta and lipid debris or, conversely, increased endolysosomal stress, lipid peroxidation, tau accumulation, and neurodegeneration, indicating that even a small set of 2 proteins can map to a mechanistically high-impact pathway when the pathway occupies a central regulatory position in brain homeostasis.

To complement this functional interpretation, we include the corresponding interaction view for the enriched protein set below. We include the protein-protein interaction network visualization and the corresponding STRING webpage link below for these 2 enriched proteins.
