![Link to the STRING webpage](https://string-db.org/cgi/link?to=823BEDDE37356EB7)

With this network-level overview in place, the following paragraphs introduce the significant proteins identified in the enrichment analysis and relate their known biology to Alzheimer disease in a cautious, mechanism-oriented manner. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.

Among the proteins listed, APOE is by far the most directly and strongly relevant to Alzheimer’s disease. Although the function provided here concerns microbial infection and hepatitis C virus biology, the underlying biology is highly pertinent to Alzheimer pathogenesis because APOE is a central regulator of lipid transport, receptor interactions, and proteoglycan-mediated cellular uptake, all of which are deeply implicated in amyloid-beta metabolism and neurodegeneration. APOE isoforms, especially APOE4, are the strongest common genetic risk factors for late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, and mechanisms involving receptor binding and cellular trafficking are thought to influence amyloid deposition, clearance, neuroinflammation, and synaptic dysfunction. The noted interaction with HSPGs is particularly interesting because HSPGs have also been implicated in amyloid aggregation and spread within the brain. In addition, the association with autophagy is noteworthy, as impaired autophagic flux is a recognized feature of Alzheimer’s disease and may contribute to the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates. Thus, even though the annotation here is framed in the context of HCV infection, it highlights core APOE properties—receptor engagement, lipid-associated particle biology, and autophagy-linked trafficking—that are mechanistically relevant to Alzheimer’s disease.[PubMed:25122793](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25122793) [PubMed:29695434](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29695434) 

In contrast to APOE, which is directly tied to genetic risk and lipid transport, SYT1 may be more informative as a marker of downstream neuronal and synaptic vulnerability. SYT1 stands out as a potentially relevant Alzheimer-associated protein because it is a core component of synaptic vesicle exocytosis and therefore directly linked to synaptic integrity, one of the earliest and most important pathological correlates of cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease. Its role as a calcium sensor for neurotransmitter release places it at the center of activity-dependent neuronal communication, which is profoundly disrupted in Alzheimer’s disease. The additional functions involving phospholipid binding and interactions with syntaxin, neurexins, and AP2 suggest broader importance in vesicle cycling, membrane trafficking, and synaptic organization. These processes are highly relevant because Alzheimer pathology is associated with synaptic vesicle dysfunction, altered calcium homeostasis, and impaired endocytic trafficking. While SYT1 is not a canonical genetic risk factor on the level of APOE, its biological role makes it a meaningful mechanistic candidate for understanding how synaptic failure develops during disease progression. In this context, SYT1 may be viewed as relevant to the downstream neuronal dysfunction that mediates memory impairment and cognitive decline.[PubMed:11242035](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11242035) [PubMed:7961887](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7961887)

### Neuronal System (REAC:R-HSA-112316) 

The neuronal system pathway encompasses the cellular and molecular processes that enable neurons and their supporting glial partners to generate, transmit, integrate, and adapt signals across brain circuits. This pathway includes synaptic vesicle cycling, neurotransmitter release and reuptake, receptor signaling, dendritic spine maintenance, axonal integrity, endosomal trafficking, proteostasis, mitochondrial homeostasis, activity-dependent plasticity, and coordinated interactions with astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and infiltrating immune cells. In the healthy brain, these processes sustain learning, memory, attention, reward processing, and higher-order cognition through a tightly regulated balance between excitation and inhibition, efficient intracellular transport, and trophic and metabolic support from non-neuronal cells. Within this framework, astrocytes regulate glutamate uptake and lactate supply, microglia monitor synapses and inflammatory tone, oligodendrocytes support axonal function and can influence amyloid precursor protein processing, and neuromodulatory neuronal populations such as cholinergic and dopaminergic neurons shape circuit performance. Because Alzheimer disease is fundamentally associated with disorders of synapses, circuits, and progressive neuronal vulnerability, the neuronal system pathway provides an integrative context that may link amyloid beta accumulation, tau pathology, neuroinflammation, altered neuronal activity states, endosomal dysfunction, selective neuronal loss, and failure of network connectivity.

Against this biological background, the collected studies suggest that the neuronal system pathway is centrally involved in Alzheimer disease because the disorder appears to emerge, at least in part, as a progressive failure of neuronal signaling, synaptic maintenance, and circuit homeostasis that is amplified by pathological interactions with glial and immune cells. Human three-dimensional culture models show that neurons, astrocytes, and microglia together recapitulate amyloid beta aggregation, phosphorylated tau accumulation, microglial recruitment, nitric oxide-mediated toxicity, axonal injury, and neuronal death, indicating that neuronal dysfunction in Alzheimer disease may be difficult to separate from multicellular neuroinflammatory signaling (PubMed:29950669). Consistent with this view, single-nucleus analysis of living human cortex identified an early cortical amyloid response in which neurons enter a transient hyperactive state before excitatory neuron loss, while microglia expand inflammatory programs and both oligodendrocytes and pyramidal neurons increase genes related to amyloid beta production and processing, placing abnormal neuronal activity and altered cell states near the beginning of disease progression (PubMed:37774681). 

This early systems-level disruption is further supported by mechanistic studies that connect neuronal system failure to altered intracellular trafficking and synaptic biology. Increased neuronal adaptor protein containing pleckstrin homology domain, phosphotyrosine binding domain, leucine zipper motif one drives early endosome enlargement, rab5 hyperactivation, altered long-term potentiation and long-term depression, basal forebrain cholinergic degeneration, and memory impairment, while genetic studies implicate Alzheimer disease risk genes affecting endosomal and synaptic function, including bin amphiphysin two and calcium modulating family member three, in conserved memory defects (PubMed:40514243, PubMed:38692279). Additional evidence shows that dose-sensitive loss of cd2 associated protein perturbs dendritic branching, spine density, proteostasis, presynaptic release, and synaptic plasticity, further supporting the view that synaptic homeostasis may represent a core node of vulnerability in Alzheimer disease (PubMed:39146503). At the circuit level, amyloid beta is associated with a mixed pattern of neuronal hyperactivity and silencing; importantly, silent neurons display severe presynaptic disconnection, spine loss, and suppressed synaptic activity, suggesting that synaptic decoupling may provide a direct route from amyloid pathology to cognitive decline (PubMed:40875806). 

Taken together, these findings lead naturally to the question of why some neuronal populations are especially susceptible whereas others appear relatively preserved. Selective vulnerability is evident across neuronal subtypes and systems: tau-associated analyses identified particularly vulnerable neuronal populations enriched for cell-death, autophagosome maturation, actin remodeling, and vesicle transport pathways, while human resilience studies found that preservation of parvalbumin-positive inhibitory neurons and other neuronal populations correlates with better cognitive status despite pathology (PubMed:40448997, PubMed:39262221). Beyond cortical excitatory neurons, degeneration of ventral tegmental area dopaminergic neurons occurs at pre-plaque stages in a mouse model and contributes to impaired hippocampal plasticity, memory, and reward processing, indicating that neuronal system disruption may extend to neuromodulatory circuits as well (PubMed:28367951). 

A further layer of complexity emerges when neuronal vulnerability is considered together with contributions from non-neuronal cells. The pathway is broadened by evidence that oligodendrocytes, in addition to neurons, produce amyloid beta and contribute to plaque formation, and that astrocyte-specific regulatory mechanisms such as loss of PR domain containing sixteen divergent transcript impair glutamate uptake, lactate release, and support for neuronal spine density, thereby worsening neuronal instability (PubMed:39103558, PubMed:39207536). Human organoid microphysiological systems additionally demonstrate that monocytes from affected individuals show increased infiltration, reduced amyloid beta clearance, heightened interleukin one beta and chemokine ligand three signaling, astrocyte activation, and neuronal apoptosis, reinforcing the possibility that neuronal system pathology in Alzheimer disease reflects convergence between intrinsic neuronal defects and extrinsic inflammatory injury (PubMed:40845091). Taken together, these publications support a model in which Alzheimer disease is closely linked to the neuronal system pathway through early activity imbalance, defective endosomal and vesicular trafficking, impaired synaptic plasticity, disrupted excitatory and inhibitory circuit organization, maladaptive glial and immune crosstalk, and selective neuronal degeneration that may ultimately contribute to memory loss and broader cognitive decline.[PubMed:29950669](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29950669) [PubMed:37774681](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37774681) [PubMed:39103558](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39103558) [PubMed:38692279](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38692279) [PubMed:28367951](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28367951) [PubMed:39207536](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39207536) [PubMed:40514243](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40514243) [PubMed:39146503](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39146503) [PubMed:39262221](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39262221) [PubMed:40448997](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40448997) [PubMed:40845091](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40845091) [PubMed:40875806](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40875806) 

In light of this literature-based context, the enrichment result can be interpreted as a focused quantitative signal within a broader disease-relevant biological framework. There were 3 Alzheimer disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the neuronal system pathway, indicating that this functional category captures a focused but biologically relevant subset of the analyzed disease-linked protein landscape. Given that the neuronal system pathway spans synaptic vesicle cycling, neurotransmitter release and reuptake, receptor signaling, dendritic spine maintenance, axonal integrity, endosomal trafficking, proteostasis, mitochondrial homeostasis, activity-dependent plasticity, and coordinated communication with astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, and infiltrating immune cells, the identification of 3 proteins within this pathway is consistent with the central role of synaptic and circuit dysfunction in Alzheimer disease. In quantitative terms, the enrichment result highlights a compact network-level signal centered on processes that directly govern learning, memory, attention, and higher-order cognition, all of which are prominently impaired during disease progression. We include below the protein-protein interaction network visualization for these 3 proteins together with the link to the Search Tool for the Retrieval of Interacting Genes and Proteins webpage for direct inspection of their interaction context.

### Transmission across Chemical Synapses (REAC:R-HSA-112315) 

Transmission across chemical synapses is a core biological process through which one neuron communicates with another by regulated neurotransmitter release from the presynaptic terminal, diffusion across the synaptic cleft, and activation of receptors and signaling machinery in the postsynaptic membrane. This pathway encompasses presynaptic vesicle docking, priming, calcium-dependent exocytosis, neurotransmitter clearance and recycling, receptor activation, postsynaptic scaffold organization, and activity-dependent plasticity mechanisms such as long-term potentiation and long-term depression. It also depends on the precise spatial alignment of presynaptic release sites with postsynaptic receptor domains, a structural organization supported by transsynaptic assemblies that physically and functionally coordinate both sides of the synapse. In the brain, this pathway supports excitatory, inhibitory, and modulatory signaling and thereby contributes to learning, memory encoding, network stability, and adaptive circuit remodeling. Because cognition depends on both efficient neurotransmission and synaptic plasticity, even subtle disturbances in glutamatergic, gamma aminobutyric acid mediated, or cholinergic synaptic transmission may have substantial consequences for memory formation and neuronal resilience. In Alzheimer disease, transmission across chemical synapses appears especially relevant because synaptic dysfunction emerges early, precedes extensive neuronal death, and may integrate multiple pathogenic influences, including amyloid beta, tau pathology, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, metal imbalance, astrocyte dysregulation, and loss of inhibitory control.

Against this biological background, the collected literature suggests that transmission across chemical synapses may represent not merely a secondary consequence of Alzheimer disease, but a central site at which molecular pathology is translated into cognitive failure. The strongest direct evidence comes from a study showing that synapses isolated from both mouse models and human Alzheimer brain are intrinsically defective in long-term potentiation, with reduced surface insertion of alpha amino three hydroxy five methyl four isoxazolepropionic acid receptors, indicating impaired capacity for activity-dependent synaptic strengthening that is fundamental for learning and memory; notably, phosphodiesterase five and phosphodiesterase nine inhibition partially rescued this defect, linking cyclic nucleotide signaling to restoration of synaptic plasticity in diseased synapses (PubMed:27986924). Systems-level studies further reinforce this interpretation by identifying chemical synaptic transmission as a recurrently enriched biological process in Alzheimer disease and across related neurodegenerative conditions, suggesting that synaptic communication may be a convergent molecular vulnerability rather than an isolated downstream event (PubMed:39392880; PubMed:31068785; PubMed:38554950). Several studies further indicate that both excitatory and inhibitory components of synaptic transmission are disrupted. In early-stage disease models, hippocampal gamma aminobutyric acid mediated transmission is reduced because of loss of parvalbumin interneurons and decreased gamma aminobutyric acid synthesis and transport, producing hyperexcitability, greater seizure susceptibility, and worsening cognitive impairment; restoration of neuregulin one signaling improved both seizure control and cognition, supporting a mechanistic link between inhibitory synaptic failure and Alzheimer-related dysfunction (PubMed:38388921). Transcriptomic analyses similarly identify altered gamma aminobutyric acid synapse genes and reduced gamma aminobutyric acid type B receptor subunit one expression in Alzheimer disease, consistent with impaired inhibitory control and network imbalance (PubMed:31068785; PubMed:40043785). At the structural level, normal synaptic function requires nanoscale transsynaptic alignment of presynaptic vesicle release machinery with postsynaptic receptor and scaffold domains, and work on transsynaptic assemblies provides a plausible anatomical framework for why even subtle disorganization of synaptic architecture could compromise neurotransmission efficiency and plasticity (PubMed:37369583). Additional evidence suggests that synaptic transmission abnormalities in Alzheimer disease may also be shaped by broader cellular and biochemical disturbances: copper dyshomeostasis may disrupt synaptic buffering during glutamatergic transmission, astrocytic calcium signaling abnormalities may impair tripartite synapse regulation and glutamate homeostasis, and hippocampal proteomic changes indicate that innate immune activation and glial responses coincide with reduced communication across chemical synapses (PMID not available for the copper review; PubMed:40585210; PubMed:38554950). The cholinergic dimension remains clinically important because current symptomatic therapies enhance neurotransmission by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, yet the broader literature suggests that Alzheimer disease involves a multisystem synaptic disorder extending beyond acetylcholine to glutamatergic, inhibitory, and neuromodulatory signaling (PMID not available for the therapeutic reviews). Overall, the pathway appears related to Alzheimer disease because synaptic transmission is among the earliest and most consistently disrupted processes in the disorder, linking molecular lesions to impaired plasticity, excitation inhibition imbalance, network dysfunction, and ultimately memory decline.[PubMed:27986924](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27986924) [PubMed:39392880](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39392880) [PubMed:38388921](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38388921) [PubMed:31068785](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31068785) [PubMed:39210294](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39210294) [PubMed:37369583](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37369583) [PubMed:40585210](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40585210) [PubMed:38554950](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38554950) [PubMed:40043785](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40043785) [PubMed:41588241](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41588241) 

Building on this literature-based context, the enrichment result provides a compact but potentially informative pathway-level signal. There were 3 Alzheimer disease-associated proteins significantly enriched in the pathway of transmission across chemical synapses, a process that represents a central biological mechanism for neuronal communication and is highly relevant to cognition because it governs neurotransmitter release, synaptic receptor activation, and activity-dependent plasticity. Given that the analyzed set contains 3 proteins, the enrichment signal is numerically compact, yet biologically meaningful, because this pathway directly aligns with one of the earliest and most quantitatively replicated features of Alzheimer disease, namely synaptic dysfunction that emerges before widespread neuronal loss and contributes substantially to memory decline and reduced network resilience. In this context, an enrichment involving 3 of 3 mapped proteins indicates that 100 percent of the proteins in this pathway-focused subset converge on a single neurobiological process that is strongly implicated in disease pathogenesis.

To complement this pathway interpretation, the network visualization below provides a protein-protein interaction view of the same 3 proteins and offers additional context for how these molecules may be functionally connected. ### axon (GO:0030424) 

The axon is the specialized elongated projection of a neuron that propagates electrical impulses from the cell body toward presynaptic terminals, thereby enabling long-range communication across neural circuits. Its structure and function depend on several tightly coordinated features, including maintenance of membrane excitability, organization of the axon initial segment where action potentials are initiated, cytoskeletal integrity for transport of organelles and proteins, vesicular and endolysosomal trafficking, and interactions with myelin and glial cells that support rapid conduction and metabolic homeostasis. Because axons can extend over long distances and rely on efficient intracellular transport and precise domain organization, they may be especially vulnerable to disturbances in protein processing, lipid balance, membrane repair, and neuroimmune interactions. In the adult brain, axonal damage has limited spontaneous recovery, so pathological changes in axonal conduction, terminal integrity, and axon-glia coupling can have major consequences for connectivity, synaptic transmission, and cognition. In Alzheimer disease, the axon has increasingly been viewed not merely as a passive victim of plaque and tau pathology, but also as an early and active site of dysfunction characterized by dystrophic swellings, impaired conduction, degeneration of long-range projections, altered myelin-axon interactions, and maladaptive remodeling of the axon initial segment.  

Against this biological background, the collected studies suggest that axonal pathology may represent a central component of Alzheimer disease pathogenesis, spanning early circuit disruption, interaction with amyloid beta and tau pathology, and later structural degeneration. A major theme is the formation of plaque-associated axonal spheroids or dystrophic neurites, which appear to be functionally important rather than purely histological byproducts. In mouse models, enlarging spheroids along axons produce action potential conduction block by acting as electrical current sinks, thereby disrupting long-range connectivity and neural network activity; this process is driven in part by endolysosomal accumulation and the lysosomal protein phospholipase D family member three, and can be ameliorated by reducing phospholipase D family member three or inhibiting mechanistic target of rapamycin signaling, supporting a possible causal role for axonal trafficking and proteostatic failure in disease-related circuit dysfunction (PubMed:36450991, PubMed:40065072). Several studies further indicate that many dystrophic neurites around plaques originate from axon terminals and are associated with abnormal extracellular vesicle accumulation, defective secretion, cytoskeletal and lipid transport abnormalities, and membrane injury with calcium elevation and calpain activation. Together, these observations place the axon as a key subcellular site where amyloid beta toxicity may be translated into structural damage and local tau phosphorylation. Consistent with this interpretation, enhancement of membrane repair by annexin A6 reduces dystrophic neurites and phospho-tau accumulation, thereby strengthening the mechanistic link between axonal injury and downstream tau-related pathology (PubMed:37172911, PubMed:37667395, PubMed:40411591).  

This axon-centered view also appears relevant at very early stages of disease progression. Loss of locus coeruleus noradrenergic axons occurs before plaque deposition in the olfactory bulb and is driven by microglial phagocytosis, producing early olfactory dysfunction, while related work in a rat model suggests that degeneration of these projections in the hippocampus triggers compensatory enhancement of beta-adrenergic receptor signaling that temporarily helps preserve plasticity and behavior in prodromal stages (PubMed:40781079, PubMed:33952633). At the level of axonal domains, both amyloid precursor protein elevation and phospho-tau accumulation are associated with structural remodeling of the axon initial segment in experimental systems and human tissue, implying that altered excitability and action potential initiation may represent additional mechanisms by which axonal dysfunction contributes to cognitive impairment independently of extracellular amyloid beta itself (PubMed:36717226, PubMed:35610289).  

From this point, the literature further suggests that axonal integrity may be difficult to separate from myelin support and neuro-glial interactions. Proteomic and imaging studies identify the myelin-axon interface as a vulnerable compartment in Alzheimer disease, with amyloid beta aggregation in periaxonal and paranodal regions, reduced paranode density, aberrant myelination, and disturbed neuro-glial signaling around dystrophic axons. Complementary experimental evidence indicates that myelin dysfunction can actively drive amyloid beta deposition by causing accumulation of amyloidogenic machinery within axonal swellings and by diverting microglia away from plaque containment, suggesting that axonal pathology may both result from and amplify core Alzheimer disease lesions (PubMed:40514588, PubMed:37258678). Biomarker studies are broadly consistent with this temporal sequence, indicating that synaptic alterations tend to emerge earlier with amyloid beta positivity, whereas axonal degeneration reflected by neurofilament light chain becomes more prominent at later tau-positive stages and correlates with worse cognition and neurodegeneration (PubMed:33279949, PubMed:40495607). Finally, the pathway may also have therapeutic relevance because axonal damage is not necessarily irreversible: promotion of secreted protein acidic and rich in cysteine-driven axonal regrowth restores hippocampal to prefrontal cortex projections and improves memory in a mouse model, while preservation of endogenous lithium homeostasis prevents axon and myelin loss, suggesting that maintaining or restoring axonal structure and conduction could be an effective strategy for modifying disease progression (PubMed:37085711, PubMed:40770094). Taken together, these publications support the view that the axon is a major anatomical and mechanistic substrate of Alzheimer disease, integrating amyloid beta toxicity, tau-associated degeneration, myelin failure, neuroimmune attack, impaired conduction, and limited regenerative responses into the progressive breakdown of brain connectivity that underlies clinical decline.[PubMed:36450991](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36450991) [PubMed:40065072](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40065072) [PubMed:37172911](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37172911) [PubMed:37667395](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37667395) [PubMed:40411591](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40411591) [PubMed:40781079](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40781079) [PubMed:33952633](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33952633) [PubMed:36717226](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36717226) [PubMed:35610289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35610289) [PubMed:40514588](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40514588) [PubMed:37258678](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37258678) [PubMed:33279949](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33279949) [PubMed:40495607](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40495607) [PubMed:37085711](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37085711) [PubMed:40770094](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40770094) 

In light of these literature-based observations, the enrichment result in the present analysis appears biologically coherent. There were proteins associated with Alzheimer disease significantly enriched in the pathway describing the axon as the specialized elongated projection of a neuron that propagates electrical impulses from the cell body toward presynaptic terminals, thereby enabling long-range communication across neural circuits. The enrichment signal is functionally consistent with core pathological features of Alzheimer disease because this pathway integrates several quantitatively important biological dimensions, including membrane excitability, organization of the axon initial segment where action potentials are initiated, cytoskeletal integrity required for intracellular transport across long cellular distances, vesicular and endolysosomal trafficking, and interactions with myelin and glial cells that support rapid conduction and metabolic homeostasis. In the context of Alzheimer disease, this enrichment is biologically notable because axons can extend across substantial anatomical distances, depend on sustained transport efficiency and precise compartmental organization, and show limited spontaneous recovery in the adult brain, making even modest disturbances in protein processing, lipid balance, membrane repair, and neuroimmune coupling potentially consequential for connectivity, synaptic transmission, and cognition. Collectively, the enriched pathway therefore supports a disease model in which axonal dysfunction is not a secondary endpoint but an early and active component of pathology, with effects spanning dystrophic swelling formation, impaired electrical conduction, degeneration of long-range projections, altered myelin-axon interactions, and maladaptive remodeling of the axon initial segment.

To further contextualize the enrichment result, the significant proteins identified in the analysis may help connect the pathway-level signal to specific disease-relevant mechanisms. During the function enrichment analysis, we identified serveral significant proteins. We will introduce them in-details in the following.  
APOE is the most notable protein in this list with respect to Alzheimer’s disease because it is one of the strongest and best-established genetic and mechanistic contributors to late-onset Alzheimer’s disease. Although the function provided here is framed in the context of microbial infection, it is highly relevant to Alzheimer biology for several reasons. First, APOE is a central regulator of lipid transport, receptor binding, and cellular uptake pathways in the brain, and these same properties underlie both its role in viral particle biology and its role in neurodegeneration. The fact that APOE mediates interactions with cell-surface receptors such as LDLr, VLDLr, and SR-B1 is particularly important because receptor-dependent trafficking and lipid homeostasis are deeply implicated in amyloid-beta aggregation, clearance, and neuronal vulnerability in Alzheimer’s disease. Second, the mention of autophagy is especially relevant, as dysregulated autophagy is increasingly recognized as a contributor to Alzheimer pathology, influencing protein clearance, amyloid processing, and neuronal survival. Thus, this infection-related function reinforces the broader concept that APOE operates at the intersection of lipid metabolism, receptor-mediated uptake, and intracellular clearance pathways, all of which are central to Alzheimer pathogenesis. More broadly, the observation that APOE can be co-opted during infection also aligns with growing interest in the relationship between host defense, neuroinflammation, and Alzheimer’s disease mechanisms. Therefore, APOE clearly stands out as the protein with the most meaningful connection to Alzheimer’s disease in the present dataset.[PubMed:25122793](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25122793) [PubMed:29695434](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29695434)
